I keep entering domains the slow way in the fastest era in history. Twice now and I'd do it again.

You can go to Claude right now and start building in a domain you have zero expertise in.

And it might work tbh, in fact, we're in the most competitive era of software in history because of that.

So why would you go into a domain you haven't earned? Go into the one where you've put the most reps in. That's your edge now.

We grew Simply Smashed to the highest rated burger in London organically and that whole experience pulled me into writing for founders at agencies. I did that for a year, which led to Draper.

With Vibenasheeds same thing. Grew a YouTube channel first, figured out what hit and what didn't, then started building.

It reminds me of something Abdel once said to me... AI gets you 60% of the way there, it's on you to fill the gap. That 60% is everything that's ever been publicly scraped. The other 40% doesn't exist in any dataset. You learn it in the arena.

England crashed out of the World Cup semis yesterday and somehow I was the happiest person in the room.

You know that scene in Avengers where Red Skull says "I guide others to a treasure I cannot possess," that's basically been my experience owning a restaurant for two years.

We built Simply Smashed to be this communal living room where people come to watch games and hang out, and I've watched hundreds of people have that exact experience but I've never actually had it myself because I'm always behind the counter or thinking about what's broken or what needs ordering.

Yesterday Sifat was running everything so I could just... sit.

I had a strawberry cheesecake milkshake and the aircon was on and the whole room was going through it together as England went out and it was genuinely one of my favourite days at the shop.

I still heard an Uber order get cancelled from across the room and it set off alarm bells in my head so it's never going to be the same as walking in fresh.

But it was close, and that was enough.

I was building an AI company between burger orders and honestly I miss it.

I keep looking at this photo and it's kinda crazy.

Simply Smashed was on its second location. Peruvian Street Kitchen was on its first. And somewhere in between both of those I decided this was also where I'd start building an AI content company on Replit.

I had my laptop wedged into whatever corner I could find, squinting at code I barely understood while delivery drivers walked in and out.

I'd be mid-prompt and someone would shout that orders were backing up so I'd get stuck in packing rice boxes and saucing them up.

Then come back to my laptop trying to remember what I was even building.

If the rush got too much the laptop just got closed and that was that.

I'd been training writers at a ghostwriting agency and I could see so clearly that the whole industry was about to flip. Like I could literally feel it. And I had this thing in my head going if I don't start building this right now, from this kitchen, on this dying laptop, someone else is going to do it and I'll be watching from behind a fryer.

It wasn't a plan btw. I didn't sit down and map anything out. Two food brands running, a kitchen that's too small for any of this, and my brain just going "yeah but what if we also built a tech company from here." I physically couldn't not do it.

That was a couple of months ago.

Draper is now past ramen profitable and growing every month. Peruvian Street Kitchen is opening its second physical location soon iA.

Everything is better now. Better setup, better tools, actual laptops that work. But I keep coming back to this photo because something about building from that kitchen felt different and I can't fully explain why.

P.S: I'm a firm believer that being in the trenches means delaying your trim, you have to earn it as a reward.

Side project of the week: I built an AI that composes music and then removes the music from itself.

vibenasheeds: the claude for making vocal nasheed beats.

Some of you might remember the lofi Muslim YouTube channel I posted about last year. I was making nasheed beats after 12-hour shifts at Simply Smashed because I could not find halal background music.

Every nasheed pack was either £30+ per beat or so rinsed that you'd hear the same track in three different Muslim creators' videos on the same day.

That whole channel was a test run... I've been cooking this up quietly between everything else.

vibenasheeds is the actual thing. You prompt the vibe you want for your scene and AI generates a full track from scratch.

Then what I'm calling the halal engine kicks in and separates the stems and strips the instruments out of the file, gone. What's left is vocals and daf.

It composes with instruments first because that's how you get something that actually sounds good, then removes them... sounds like a weird extra step but the output is better (and I spent an embarrassing amount of time looking).

The thing about the nasheed scene right now is the creators in it are incredible. I grew up watching them figure out an entire genre from scratch with basically nothing.

You ever watch Chris Howett cycling through the mountains of Switzerland on an electric scooter? Half of why that youtube content hits the way it does is the audio. Muslim creators have been locked out of that entire dimension, you're either using the same 50 beats as everyone else or you're working in silence and hoping the visuals carry it.

I want to describe what I'm hearing in my head for a specific moment and have it exist.

Link in comments to try it out!

I built the highest rated burger joint in London. Last month I walked into one that made me take notes.

I had a stopover in Sweden, hadn't slept, needed a meal. Searched for halal options and this place popped up. Highest rated burger joint in Gothenburg. Smash burgers. I couldn't not go.

The owner was North African, Algerian I think. The food was properly good. But the thing I'm still thinking about weeks later isn't the burger.

Next to the counter they had coffee and these homemade North African biscuits laid out. Free. Take as many as you want. You could tell someone had made them that morning.

People remember experiences. The burger was great but it's the coffee and the biscuits I keep coming back to. It's never the main thing. It's the thing next to the main thing that nobody asked for.

Content is product. Product is content.

I've said it maybe 200 times now. Most founders nod and then go do the opposite anyway.

We ran Simply Smashed with zero paid marketing. Literally zero. We were just documenting the messiness of building a burger joint from the back of a flower shop and posting it, and that was doing the job a £5k/month ad budget would've done. We became the highest-rated burger spot in London and never boosted a single post.

Then MiniDeed happened. The product was good and the impact was real and nobody knew it existed. The thing about having no distribution is it doesn't matter how good your product is. Nobody sees it.

Completely opposite outcomes that somehow taught me the exact same thing.

The founders who get this are building content into the product from day one. The GTM isn't a department you bolt on in month six, it's the whole thing.

If you just raised and you're trying to decide whether to invest in content or put it off, the thing you're actually deferring is distribution.

We raised £26,000 for charity through an app where every like was worth 1p.

We made exactly £0 in revenue.

I was 18. First year of my degree apprenticeship at Goldman Sachs.

I met the co-founder in the basement prayer room. We'd just finished praying and I asked him how he was doing, just being polite, and he mistook it as me asking how the app was doing.

This man was probably mid-thirties, been at Goldman for years, and he just started telling me about this social media platform where every like triggered a micro-donation to charity.

I had no idea what he was talking about. But I was in.

That's how MiniDeed started for me. 1p, 2p, 5p. Tiny amounts that added up across 25 countries over two years. We onboarded Islamic Relief, Human Relief Foundation, a bunch of smaller orgs. We got featured in The New Arab. And somehow built a community where people were opening up about mental health because the whole vibe was just different. Users told us it was the only app where they felt safe doing that.

Honestly watching the live donation ticker go up was more addictive than any MRR dashboard I've looked at since (and I say that as someone who now stares at dashboards for a living).

We never figured out how to make money from it. Donations still trickle through the app daily, years later. But it was my first real taste of building something and I think about it all the time.

18 years old, sitting in Goldman Sachs by day, shipping a charity app by night. It led me to build the highest-rated burger joint in London. And now Draper.

I built the highest rated burger joint in London. 4.9 stars, 3000+ reviews.
Those two years taught me more about building than any MBA ever could.

The thing about the food industry is nothing is theoretical. From day one you're making decisions with real money on razor thin margins. One bad weekend and you feel it in your bank account by Friday, not next quarter.

→ We got burgled
→ I dealt with literal fires
→ One supplier issue and the whole menu changes overnight
→ I had staff not show up while I was two hours away with no way to get back
→ You learn to read people very quickly because you genuinely don't have time not to

Simply Smashed started from a kitchen we were already using and maybe £100 on a new grill. That was the entire business plan.

When every pound counts you develop this instinct for what's worth spending on and what isn't. That instinct doesn't go away when you move into tech. It just gets applied differently.

Every decision I make building Draper now, whether it's hiring, spending, prioritising, I can trace back to something I learned in that kitchen. That's not from a textbook, it's from a Friday night that went sideways.

And honestly I'd take someone who's survived a Friday night service with half their staff missing over someone who's only ever seen pressure in a case study.

It's the most expensive MBA that I never paid for tbh

Let's address the elephant in the room - most AI content is garbage. Here’s why:

LLMs copying from other LLM generated articles. Repurposed slop from Reddit dressed up as insights. You can feel it when you're scrolling. It all sounds the same.

But here's what I've learned about content that actually works after working with YC and A16z founders.

When Simply Smashed took off, it wasn't because we posted more than anyone else. It was because we told our story. In our voice. People could feel the difference. That's why they kept showing up.

The founders I worked with who won - same thing. Their story, told properly, compounding over time.

The thing is, most founders don't have time for this. They're building. You can't cook with one hand on a phone trying to document yourself. You need both hands in the work.

That's what me and Mustafa kept talking about. Builders should be focused on building. AI should be documenting you cooking.

That's what we're building with Draper.

Right now the human taste is us. We work with founders closely to get their voice right. But we're codifying what we've learned into systems. The vision is the human taste becomes you. Your stories. Your voice. The way you actually talk.

Not repurposed slop. But actual authentic human stories that's told at scale.

Right now we're deep in LinkedIn. But the vision is bigger. Content engines for entire teams, not just founders. Content marketing is shifting on how companies attract customers, investors and talent (will share more on this soon). We're building the infrastructure to make it scalable.

I've been lying to you.

Every time you saw me at Simply Smashed, there was something I wasn't telling you.

For the last two years while I was running the restaurant, I was also advising Series A founders on their content strategy. Part time, on the side, mostly in secret.

I was on calls with YC founders and A16z portfolio companies, founders building companies that will be household names in five years.

And I was taking those calls from my restaurant.

There's this memory I keep coming back to. I'm on a call with a founder talking positioning, narrative strategy, how to become the voice of their space. Elite player. The kind of person you'd expect to be advising from some nice office somewhere.

And I'm standing next to our Simply Smashed punching machine.

I had to be on site that day. Couldn't leave. So I just found a corner, put my noise-cancelling headphones on, and took the call anyway.

My resume said: Restaurant Owner.

My calendar said: Strategy Call with a16z Portfolio Company.

They had no idea where I was. Most people didn't know I was doing this at all.

Here's how that even happened.

When Simply Smashed took off, people started asking how we did it. Highest rated burger joint in London with no marketing budget. Pure organic storytelling.

My brother saw it before I did.

He introduced me to someone at a content strategy agency - the kind that works with YC founders and a16z portfolio companies. They were looking for someone. My brother knew this was exactly what I'd been doing without realising it.

That someone was Mustafa Khan, ACA. Who would end up becoming my co-founder.

I said yes immediately. Everything I'd learned at Simply Smashed was from first principles. Pure instinct. I wanted to see what this looked like at scale with the smartest founders in the world.

That became my arena.

I started advising founders. Got them over 25M+ views across X and LinkedIn Then I got promoted to Head of Training. Responsible for training writers and creative directors on how to do what I'd been doing on gut feel alone.

And it fit like a glove.

Looking back, the thread was always there. Every project I've ever worked on grew through storytelling. I just didn't have words for what I was doing. It was instinct compounding over years.

Last year I left the agency with Mustafa.

We're building Draper.

AI agents plus human taste for founder storytelling.

Same instinct that's been compounding this whole time. Same playbook that took a burger joint to number one. Now we're helping other founders do it for their companies.

I smuggled a burger into the Emirates for my first ever Arsenal game.
Had 2 friends help me set up the shot got us viral.

So there I am in the back of an Uber. Double wagyu. Caramelised onions. The works. Steam creeping out of the foil, driver clocking me in the mirror every thirty seconds.

He doesn't ask. I don't explain.

47 minutes to kickoff. East London to the Emirates. Praying the smell doesn't get me caught at the gates.

I grew up watching Arsenal on dodgy streams. Dreamed about this stadium my whole life.

Normal person would just enjoy the moment.

I couldn't help myself.

There's an account called Footy Scran. Half a million followers. They feature stadium food from across the country. One post can do more for a brand than a year of ads.

Simply Smashed isn't inside the Emirates.

That's when I knew what I had to do.

Security didn't blink. Walked straight through with a burger stuffed in my jacket, heart pounding, trying to look casual.

Found my seat. Unwrapped it slowly. Steam curling up into the cold night air. The pitch glowing under the floodlights behind me.

My mate grabbed his phone.

One shot.

Tagged Footy Scran.

They reposted within hours.

Verdict: Scran.

Then the comments started flying in.

"Where is this? I've been coming here 10 years."

"How have I missed this?"

"Need this immediately."

1,800 likes on mine. 1,600 on theirs. Zero ad spend. One burger. One Uber across the city.

People ask why I couldn't just enjoy the game.

Because my brain doesn't work that way. I don't see a stadium. I see half a million people I haven't reached yet. I don't see a burger. I see a story nobody else is telling.

Most opportunities aren't hidden. They're ignored because they seem too silly to work.

Arsenal won that night. We're in the Champions League now. And the Emirates still doesn't have proper halal options.

So until that changes?

I'll be the guy in the stands with a burger in his jacket and a plan in his head.

Arsenal Football Club, if you're reading this: 3,400 likes say the demand is already there.

Your move. I'll bring the wagyu.

PS sorry about the dodgy streams ;)

Someone spent £100 trying to sabotage my stealth launch.
And honestly? It's hilarious.

So we're quietly testing PSK (Peruvian Street Kitchen). Not advertising. Just fulfilling random orders.

Day 1: This guy orders from Simply Smashed. We go all out - extra portions, made with love, the works.

Check the app that night: 1 star.

Day 2: SAME GUY orders from PSK.

Wait. We're in stealth mode. How did he even find both brands?

Whatever. We try even harder. Make it perfect.

That night: Another 1 star.

Then the smoking gun:

Someone left a 1-star Google review. On our brand new listing. Two hours after I created it.

We hadn't even taken a single order yet.

That's when I knew. This wasn't about the food.

After that, this guy starts trying to order from BOTH brands. Every. Single. Day.

Since leaving those 1-star reviews, he's attempted nearly £100 worth of orders. We just keep rejecting them.

The Uber Eats account manager was like "yeah you can just ban him" so casually. Like this happens all the time.

Because it does.

The food business is weirdly tribal. There's literally takeaway wars happening up north right now. Actual wars. Over chicken shops.

When I first started Simply Smashed, this stuff destroyed me.

I'd see a fake review and spiral. Question everything. Lose sleep wondering what I did wrong. Check the reviews obsessively. Let it consume my whole day.

My confidence would shatter. I'd second-guess every decision.

Now?

I recognise the pattern immediately. Competitor sees you doing well. Competitor panics. Competitor attacks.

It's actually validation.

Someone is SO pressed about our quiet little test that they're burning their own money AND time stalking our Google listings.

The shift happened when I realised: You can't control the tribal nonsense. You can only control the food you make and how you treat real customers.

Their panic is just noise. Your focus is the signal.

These days when I see this behaviour, I don't spiral. I smile.

Because if someone's willing to spend £100 trying to stop you...

You must be doing something right.

Anyway, we're thinking of adding him to our loyalty programme.

At this rate, he'll get a free meal by Tuesday.

Running burgers and rice boxes from the same kitchen is absolute chaos.

Found that out the hard way yesterday.

PSK's first pop-up. Simply Smashed still firing orders. Two brands, one kitchen, complete madness at 2pm.

We opened an hour late.

People waited.

Nobody left.

Once we found our flow though? Different story. Orders flying out. Both brands running smooth. The team locked in.

Then we sold out an hour early. Despite overstocking by 40%.

I've been personally messaging everyone who came. The responses are keeping me up:

"Never going Shah's again"
"1000/10 - just regret not ordering more"
"Let me know if we can invest"

That last one got me. Two weeks ago PSK was just an idea. Yesterday someone wanted to invest.

My mum's still handmaking our sauces. Every batch. Won't let anyone else touch them yet.

That's how we build brands. With our own hands first. Learning every detail. Every process. Every standard.

Running multiple brands from one kitchen isn't new for us. But when both are firing at full speed? That's when you really feel it. The pressure. The energy. The buzz when it all clicks.

This week, we announce PSK's first permanent location.

The chaos was worth it though. Every single second. Because those messages? That's what makes all the behind-the-scenes work worth it.

London - thank you for waiting that extra hour. Thank you for believing in what we're building.

I abandoned my restaurant mid-service to bike across London while my kitchen was on fire.

"Just sell chicken burgers until I get back," I told my team.

Then I ran out the door.

The cables had just burst into flames. Smoke filling the kitchen. My dad took one look at the melting electrical panel and rattled off exactly what I needed from Screwfix.

So there I was - racing through 20 London lanes on a Santander bike, while customers wondered why beef burgers suddenly went "out of stock."

They never knew their food was delayed because the owner literally abandoned them.

2 hours later, we were back online.

That was Simply Smashed, 14 months ago.

Last month, I found myself in another kitchen. Different location. New menu. Same game.

But this time, when I flipped the switches, checked the electrical loads, and fired up the grills - no panic. No surprises. Just muscle memory from 14 months of controlled chaos.

PSK - Peruvian Street Kitchen - went from idea to serving customers in 2 weeks.

Not because we rushed. Because we already knew every shortcut. Every supplier's direct line. Every permit loophole. Every mistake to avoid.

The same hands that once scrambled to fix burning cables now move with precision. Set up stations. Test recipes. Train staff. Like we've done this dance a hundred times.

Because we have.

The early reviews are proving what experience tastes like:

"Addictive"
"Can't stop thinking about it"
"When can I order again?"

Every crisis at Simply Smashed was tuition for PSK. Every fire we put out taught us how to build something fireproof.

This Sunday, November 2nd, PSK takes over Simply Smashed Stepney for one day only.

The kitchen that caught fire 14 months ago now houses something built from those ashes.

And we're still here, cooking.

A dad tried to buy chicken and rice from me 5 times in one week.
We were closed every single time.

His son had spotted PSK on my Twitter. Said it was "better than Shah's and Pepe's." In their house, that's high praise.

See, this father and son talk about everything. Football. Work. Life. But especially food. It's their language.

So when the son mentioned this new spot just around the corner from their house, the dad made a mental note.

Monday: Walked over. Closed.
Tuesday: Tried again. Closed.
Wednesday: Third attempt. Still closed.
Thursday: Fourth time. Nothing.

Each time he went home empty-handed. Each time he could've given up.

Any other dad orders Deliveroo. Moves on.

Not this one.

Friday, attempt number five. He sees our gate open. Walks up to the building - door open. Reaches our kitchen door. Lights on inside.

"Are you actually open? Can I buy food?"

We'd been operating limited hours. Testing. Perfecting. Missing customers like him all week.

Here's where it gets worse: we'd just sold our last portion. Fresh batch would take 30 minutes.

I told him straight. Expected him to leave.

"I'll wait. I'm not going home empty-handed."

So he waited. In our little kitchen. Watching us prep.

30 minutes later, he left with two boxes. One for his son. One for himself.

That night, a father and son connected over chicken and rice.

Here's the thing:

No one should have to try 5 times to taste what we're building.

That's why on November 2nd, PSK is doing a one-day pop-up at Simply Smashed Stepney.

One day. Full menu. Three sauces. The chicken and rice that's about to change London's lunch game.

No more closed doors. No more missed connections. No more "we just ran out."

Just the most addictive chicken and rice box you've ever had.

November 2nd. Simply Smashed Stepney.

Come see what that father waited for.

Come taste what London's been missing.

I'm typing this with a bandaged finger and burnt hands.

Yesterday my brother Sifat and I ran the entire Peruvian Street Kitchen ourselves. No staff. Just us. Invite-only testing that turned into our busiest "quiet" evening yet.

Someone rated us "11 out of 10." We sold out. We weren't even supposed to be open.

But here's what happened that matters more than the sales:

The first batch of chicken I grilled wasn't right. Not the standard I'd been hitting at home. Too rushed. Wrong char. By batch three, I'd found the rhythm. By batch five, it was perfect.

If I'd hired someone to run that grill yesterday, I'd never have known:
Why quality drops during a rush
Which corners get cut under pressure
What muscle memory needs to develop
How the kitchen flows when orders stack up

I see food founders all the time who think they can outsource from day one. Hire a chef. Hire managers. Never touch the grill themselves.

Then they wonder why their food tastes different six months later. Why quality slides. Why their reviews drop.

You can't train someone to maintain standards you've never held yourself.

You can't teach someone to handle pressure you've never felt.

You can't build a food business without burning your own hands first.

My brother was filling rice boxes at lightning speed. I was cutting Peruvian chicken with a bleeding finger. We moved like we did in Simply Smashed's early days - pure instinct, no waste, complete sync.

This is what being in the arena means.

Not watching from the sidelines with a clipboard. Not managing from a laptop. Actually burning yourself on the same grill your team will use tomorrow.

Now I'm boarding a flight with bandaged fingers and the smell of charcoal in my clothes heading to work on another project.

But I know exactly what our future staff will face. Exactly where they'll struggle. Exactly how to train them.

Because I bled for it first.

That's how you build something real.

I almost watched my 60-year-old dad fall off a ladder yesterday.

All for a sticker.

He was three stories up, no harness, leaning at an angle that made my stomach drop. My brother was holding the base. I was holding my breath.

"Get down," I shouted.
"I do it myself," he shouted back.

The Simply Smashed sticker needed to go up. But this wasn't our usual spot. This wasn't our usual anything.

Two years. One kitchen. Thousands of smashed burgers.

That's been our story.

Until today.

Last week I cut my finger deep enough to see white.
Today my dad's risking his neck for vinyl adhesive.

We've had offers to grow faster. Franchise inquiries. Investors. The "scale quickly" playbook.

But watching him up there - applying that second sticker way better than my rushed first one - I understood something:

The families that build things that last are the ones who never stop doing the hard work themselves.

My sticker had bubbles. His was perfect.
My hands were shaking. His were steady.

Both stickers are up now. One say Simply Smashed. The other marks something new.

Our regulars have no idea what's coming.

More soon.

One engineering student pointed a £20 webcam at a Carrom board.

Then something clicked about why young people have nowhere to go.

I was judging at Hulm's hackathon yesterday.

This student was using computer vision to auto-score Carrom - imagine pool played with your fingers, flicking coins into corner pockets on a wooden board.

Another team added pressure-sensitive gloves to track flick power.
A third built connection games between rounds.

But watching them build, I recognised something from building Simply Smashed.

Every Friday, the same problem:

"Where we watching the match?"

Pubs require drinking. Cafes close at 7. Everywhere else feels wrong.

So we had nowhere.

These students weren't just modernising a dusty board game.

They were creating spaces where you don't have to choose between your culture and being cool.

Between your values and belonging.

That's why we put a punching machine in Simply Smashed.
That's why they're putting sensors on their grandad's game.

Same hunger. Different solutions.

We're all digging up experiences buried under "that's not how it's done anymore."

Making them ours again.

The revelation?

Not one team asked "is Carrom worth saving?"

They just started building.

No permission. No validation. No waiting for someone else to fix it.

To the teams: Pick one feature. Perfect it. Then add the next.

But you already know what most people don't:

When the world doesn't have space for you, you don't complain.

You create.

Every Muslim creator faces the same impossible choice.
Use mainstream beats that compromise your values, or create content in silence.

I felt this firsthand running Simply Smashed. We had a strict no-music policy, but how do you create engaging content without sound? How do you build atmosphere in your restaurant when customers walk in?

Ever had 20 litres of white sauce spill all over your car?

I was transporting it to the restaurant when we realised the container wasn’t sealed properly. The sauce spilled everywhere. Twenty litres, gone.

It felt like a disaster, but we couldn’t salvage the sauce—so we salvaged the situation. Right there, amidst the chaos, we started shooting content. We recorded the mess, the frustration, the absurdity of it all—and then we shared it.

That content went viral. Hundreds of thousands of views on TikTok and Instagram. What started as a disaster turned into one of our most successful marketing moments.

But the story doesn’t end there. One of my staff recommended his friend’s detailing business to clean up the car, and these boys did such an incredible job that I ended up hiring two of them for front-of-house at Simply Smashed. One of them, just last month, brought in over 100 five-star reviews by himself.

When life gives you lemons, make marketing content. Setbacks have a way of leading to unexpected wins. Like the time we raised over £4,000 for charity after getting review-bombed—but that’s a story for another post.
